newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council endorses European troops for Albania.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council endorses European troops for Albania.

text.p: Moving swiftly, the U.N. Security Council gave a green light for Italy to organise and send a multinational force to Albania for at least three months to guard deliveries of food and other aid.
Italy's ambassador, Paulo Fulci, who requested that the council authorise the operation his country will lead, said after the vote late on Friday that he expected the mission to begin quickly.
He said Albania had only about a week's worth of food left. Any such venture had risks "but if you feed the people they are less nervous on an empty stomach," he said.

The Council vote was was 14 to 0 with China abstaining on a resolution that invoked Chapter 7 of the U.N. Charter, which permits the use of force. In this case, the resolution said force could be used in self-defence in warding off violence in the Balkan state, which seemed to be sliding into anarchy.

Plans, however, are still not firm on which countries will join the military mission. The resolution did not specify a number of troops. Italy previously said it expected 2,500, with the same amount of soldiers in reserve should they be needed.
France, Portugal, Spain, Greece, Turkey, Romania and Austria have expressed some willingness to send personnel. The United States, Britain and Germany will not participate.

China's representative told the council that Beijing disapproved of a resolution that allowed the use of force and that the crisis in Albania was an internal affair. But Quin Huasun said he did not use his veto to stop the operation because of the request for help from the Albanian government.

The mandate of the force -- approved by, but not under U.N. auspices -- runs for three months at which time the council can decide whether it should be extended. The operation will be financed by participating nations.

Its purpose, the resolution said, was to "facilitate the safe and prompt delivery of humanitarian assistance and to help create a secure environment for the missions of international organisations in Albania."

Albania was swept by violence in January when a string of popular savings schemes collapsed, erasing millions of dollars. Rebels seized the south in March in an armed insurrection, blaming President Sali Berisha for the fiasco and demanding that he quit.
Since then gangs have roamed the south, stealing, looting, killing and creating a food crisis, prompting the government to ask for foreign military assistance.
The resolution also stressed that the crisis in Albania was a threat to peace in the region, a veiled reference to fears of another Balkan war if unrest spills over the border.

Hostilities have flared frequently in Serbia's Kosovo province to the north where 1.2 million Albanians live. To the east, Albanians constitute about a quarter of the population in the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia where U.S. troops lead a United Nations peacekeeping operation.

The council's action follows a Vienna meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which agreed to establish a civilian mission to support democracy and elections, expected in June.
But the 54-nation body, reflecting divisions among its members, did not authorise foreign police or troops, saying the Security Council needed to give the mission a green light.
Seven members of the 15-seat Security Council belong to the OSCE -- France, Britain, Russia and the United States, Sweden, Portugal and Poland.
Whether or not the troops guarding Albanian ports would prevent refugees from leaving is not clear.

Many Albanians have sought asylum in Italy, which on Monday decided to turn away boats heading towards southeast Italian ports across the Adriatic, a journey already made by some 12,000 people since March 13.
